transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-11-19 10:30 PST
Duration: ~64 minutes
Attendees (recording): Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Kapoor (Redwood SE), Jordan Mills (Redwood), Samir Iqbal (Helix ML Platform), Lauren Cho (Helix SRE), Michael Troy (Helix Bench), Ana Ruiz (Helix Security)

Summary:
Quick technical deep-dive on throughput tuning for an on-prem/private deployment: continuous batching knobs, max_num_seqs, token limits, backpressure and redispatch behavior, interaction with KV cache hit rate and quantization tradeoffs. Goal: give Helix actionable scheduler settings and a microbenchmark plan to validate SLOs.

Topics covered:
- baseline infra (8x A100 + 2 nodes for control plane) and target: 25k tokens/s sustained, 90th pctl latency < 150ms for short queries
- continuous batch window and packer heuristics, explicit max_num_seqs, token guards per-request
- backpressure: how the scheduler detects congestion, redispatch thresholds and preemption behavior
- KV cache warmup, eviction policy impact on effective throughput
- quantization tradeoffs at 4-bit versus int8 on latency and sample quality
- networking/VPC implications for private deployment and cold-starts

Transcript body (auto-generated, medium quality — some words may be off):
[00:00] Alex (Redwood): all right hi everyone thanks for making time, we wanted to keep this focused on the scheduler and throughput knobs for your on-prem run. quick roll call?
[00:10] Samir (Helix): Samir here, Lauren, Michael and Ana are on. thanks alex, excited, we hit some weird egress spikes and stalls during last POC.
[00:18] Priya (Redwood SE): hey, Priya. quick note, we're going to call out max_num_seqs a few times — folks also call that max seqs or max concurrent sequences in other runtimes — same thing.
[00:27] Lauren (Helix): got it. we have an 8xA100 pod with 1.5TB host ram, k8s 1.25, and we've been using a 1s batching window in the pilot which seems to cause long queuing.
[00:36] Jordan (Redwood): 1s is fairly wide for low-latency SLOs, yeah.
[00:40] Michael (Helix): when we tightened the window to 200ms throughput dropped but latency improved — but not linearly, weirdly.
[00:48] Priya: that's likely due to KV cache coldness + packer inefficiency — if the packer holds short requests waiting for long ones you can see pickups that reduce throughput. Also token limits per-request matter, we saw some requests with 2k token max that stall the batch.
[00:59] Samir: can you explain the token caps interaction? we thought the server just slices.
[01:05] Priya: tokens are your per-request max generation length; if you set a high token cap the scheduler keeps the slot reserved until that request completes. continuous batching tries to interleave, but long docs can monopolize the sequence if max_num_seqs is high.
[01:16] Alex: to add — there are two levers: max_num_seqs (how many concurrent live sequences per GPU) and token_guard (per-request token cap). for throughput you usually lower max_num_seqs to avoid head-of-line blocking, and enforce tighter token_guards for interactive workloads.
[01:28] Lauren: what's a typical starting point? we want to sustain 25k tokens/s but 90p < 150ms for queries ~30-60 tokens.
[01:36] Priya: start with max_num_seqs = 128 on an A100-80GB class pod for that profile, continuous batch window 100-250ms, token_guard = 128 for interactive routes. That's a ballpark; depends on model size and KV cache hit rate.
[01:46] Michael: ok but our model is a 30B fine-tuned transformer, two kv cache shards, we saw 30-40% KV hit rate in first tests. will that kill throughput?
[01:56] Priya: yes, low KV hit rate increases memory ops and stalls. increasing cache warmup or enabling prefix caching for repeated prompts helps. Also set kv_cache_eviction = LRU with hot-set pin for small contexts you care about.
[02:06] Samir: any config flags we should watch for in private deploy? we run the control plane in the VPC and data plane in the same subnet.
[02:12] Jordan: set the rpc timeout higher during initial cache warmup (we default to 20s in hosted but you can bump to 40s for on-prem network variance). Also enable connection pooling between router and runtime to reduce TCP churn.
[02:21] Ana (Helix Security): curious about the telemetry — does Redwood expose token-level traces? we need auditability without exporting payloads.
[02:29] Alex: yes we emit token-level counters and latency histograms but payloads are redacted by default for sensitive work — you can integrate with your KMS to keep logs encrypted at rest.
[02:36] Michael: earlier you mentioned redispatch. what triggers that, and can it cause extra latency?
[02:42] Priya: redispatch occurs when a request is queued longer than redispatch_threshold (configurable). The scheduler will attempt to move the request to another GPU with free sequences. If the scheduler moves it across nodes it's best-effort and you can see a small extra latency spike (network + setup). For strict SLOs we recommend local preemption and avoiding cross-node redispatch unless necessary.
[02:58] Samir: preemption? like evicting a low-priority sequence to make room?
[03:03] Priya: exactly. Redwood supports priority classes; when high-priority interactive requests arrive, the scheduler can preempt a lower-priority batch to free max_num_seqs slots. Preemption algorithms are tunable — time-slice preempt versus immediate kill. For customer workloads we suggest graceful preempt (time-slice) to avoid corrupt partial outputs.
[03:19] Lauren: what about continuous batching heuristics — is there an adaptive window?
[03:24] Jordan: yes, there's an adaptive batch window that expands when throughput is low and contracts under high QPS. It's governed by target_latency and target_tokens_per_batch. If you set target_latency to 100ms the window will try to balance to meet that. Beware edge cases where bursts cause the window to occasionally overshoot.
[03:38] Michael: we saw a case where the window grew to 800ms during a warmup and caused p99 spikes. how to prevent?
[03:44] Priya: set max_batch_window = 250ms in addition to target_latency — that caps runaway expansion. Also set window_decay to 0.5 so it shrinks faster after spikes.
[03:53] Samir: any guidance on quantization? we'd like int8 for cost but worried about quality regressions.
[03:58] Priya: quant helps throughput significantly, int8 on A100 gives ~20-30% latency improvement for large models but watch out for per-token quality drop and potential hallucination increase. We usually recommend running an eval suite of representative prompts to quantify impact. For aggressive throughput, 4-bit QAT or GPTQ variants can give huge perf wins but need careful QA.
[04:18] Ana: from a security standpoint, do quantized models leak more or less info?
[04:22] Alex: quantization is model internal; it doesn't change telemetry or logging. Leakage risk is tied to model training/data rather than quant scheme. But obviously validate on your PII prompt sets.
[04:30] Michael: back to knobs: you mentioned max_num_seqs = 128 for our hardware. can you show the tradeoff curve — lower increases latency but higher increases throughput until you hit memory or kernel contention?
[04:42] Priya: yes, think of it as convex. Up to a point, adding concurrent sequences increases GPU utilization and throughput; beyond that, context-switches and KV cache pressure reduce per-token efficiency and latency jumps. We provided an example curve in the pilot deck (link shared) — but we'll send a tuned spreadsheet with specific toggles and expected throughput/latency bands.
[04:57] Samir: can we dynamically change max_num_seqs per route? we have both chat and long-form generations.
[05:03] Jordan: yes, route-level overrides exist. You can set route.max_num_seqs and route.token_guard to tune per-endpoint. We also support autoscaling policies that increase/decrease capacity and adjust max_num_seqs cluster-wide during business hours.
[05:15] Lauren: what about token guards per customer tenant? do we have per-tenant isolations?
[05:20] Alex: yes, tenant-level quotas and per-tenant guard rails — you can also reserve sequences per-tenant to guarantee minimum throughput.
[05:26] Michael: earlier you mentioned redispatch_threshold; what's a safe starting value?
[05:30] Priya: 250ms is common — if a request sits in queue >250ms try to move it. For strict low-latency routes you can lower to 100-150ms or disable cross-node redispatch.
[05:41] Samir: our network has occasional 30-50ms jitter between nodes. will redispatch misfire?
[05:46] Priya: that's why we recommend node affinity for ultra-low-latency routes; set prefer_local = true and only allow cross-node if local queue > backup_threshold.
[05:55] Michael: about KV cache — is there a way to prioritize hot sets and avoid eviction during spikes?
[06:00] Priya: yes run a small pinlist for prefixes that matter, or configure a hot_set_size parameter; also increase kv_cache_provisioning to reduce eviction churn. Pinning consumes memory though so balance accordingly.
[06:10] Samir: any instrumentation we should collect during microbench?
[06:13] Priya: collect: per-GPU utilization, per-sequence latency, batch sizes, KV hit rate, redispatch counts, preemptions, and RPC latencies. We'll provide a Grafana dashboard template.
[06:22] Michael: let's talk about a failure mode we hit — long requests causing starvation of short interactive requests even though we had priorities set. why?
[06:29] Jordan: common cause is long requests were pinned to sequences with realtime priority mistakenly lower, or token_guard was disabled on those routes. Also if continuous batching merges long and short into same batch, short requests wait. Solution: route affinity + token_guard + separate priority class, or enable sequence segregation: long_request_buckets.
[06:45] Samir: sequence segregation?
[06:47] Priya: split the pool logically: set max_num_seqs_per_bucket {interactive:80, long-run:48} so they don't compete. This is a good pattern for mixed workloads.
[06:56] Lauren: do we need different quant settings per bucket?
[07:00] Priya: you can; long-run can use 4-bit aggressive quant to save cost while interactive uses int8 for slightly better quality/latency. The runtime supports model variants and dynamic routing to variants.
[07:10] Alex: quick note on on-prem deploy defaults: we bake in safer defaults (lower max_num_seqs) to avoid noisy neighbor issues in multi-tenant clusters. Customers frequently increase after benching.
[07:20] Michael: can we get a sample config for the segregation + redispatch threshold + token guards?
[07:24] Priya: we'll attach a sample config in the tuning spreadsheet. Example snippet in the deck: route: chat: max_num_seqs=80, token_guard=128, prefer_local=true; route: long: max_num_seqs=48, token_guard=1024, allow_redispatch=false.
[07:38] Samir: about logging/traces — when redispatch moves a request, is that linkable back to request id? we need end-to-end trace.
[07:45] Jordan: yes every request has a UUID and the router emits an event on redispatch with old_node/new_node and timestamps. You'll see it in the audit trail.
[07:52] Ana: any compliance notes for private deploy? we need to validate that logs do not leak payloads to telemetry endpoints in the cloud.
[07:59] Alex: for private, the control plane can be air-gapped and telemetry shipped to your internal splunk; Redwood only receives anonymized counters if you opt-in. We'll include the security pack.
[08:09] Michael: let's propose a bench plan live now — cold start, warm cache, mixed QPS, long-tail latency. what's minimal sample size?
[08:17] Priya: run 5k requests per scenario for stable metrics, include a steady-state sustained run of 10 minutes for throughput. Log raw traces.
[08:25] Samir: ok we'll do that.
[08:27] Alex: any other questions before we wrap?
[08:29] Lauren: one more: is there a simple metric to watch for early warning of head-of-line blocking?
[08:33] Priya: watch redispatch_count rising and median batch sizes suddenly increasing; also a growing variance in per-seq latency is a tell.
[08:40] Michael: and set alert if kv_cache_hitrate falls below 60% for any 5m window.
[08:45] Priya: yes that's a good SRE alert.
[08:48] Samir: great — appreciate the pragmatic knobs.
[08:51] Alex: recap of next steps: Priya send tuning spreadsheet and sample config; Michael run bench and upload traces; Alex schedule follow-up. We'll also share a short how-to on pinning hot prefixes.
[08:59] Jordan: I'll also include a sample Grafana dashboard and query snippets for redispatch/preempt counts.
[09:06] Ana: thanks, security will review the pack once it's in.
[09:09] Samir: thanks everyone.
[09:12] (end)
